the study of the evolution of a part of the Western Liguria Flysch Unit (NW Italy).
the reconstruction of the paleogeographic evolution of the Western Mediterranean region during the Late Cretaceous-Paleogene.

the Western Ligurians represent a large accretionary wedge that developed during the Upper Cretaceous and Paleogene, which was progressively shifted toward the European continent during the collisional phases of the Alpine orogenesis.
the Ligurian Flysh Units represent an accretionary complex of Cretaceous-Paleogene age that was overthrust onto a paleo-European continental shelf during the Eocene.
the Western Ligurians Flysch Units are the result of the accretion of the Ligurian oceanic crust onto the European continental margin during the Alpine orogenesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Western Ligurians Flysch is a complex of Upper Cretaceous and Paleogene sedimentary rocks, which were involved in the Alpine orogenetic process and were overthrust on the paleo-European margin during the Eocene.

the Western Ligurians represent a complex accretionary wedge that evolved during the Upper Cretaceous-Paleogene, when it was accreted onto the European continental margin during the Alpine orogenetic cycle, as a result of the collision between the European and Adriatic micro-plates.
the Western Ligurians represent a typical accretionary wedge, with the main difference that they were not overthrust on the European margin during the Eocene, but during the Late Oligocene.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a better understanding of the evolution of accretionary wedges requires a detailed analysis of the processes operating in the fore-arc and in the accretionary wedge itself, and not only in the subduction channel.
the Western Ligurians are a typical accretionary complex that developed during the Cretaceous-Paleogene in the Ligurian Ocean, in front of the European continental margin.

the Western Liguride units are a unique example of the evolution of a pre-collisional accretionary wedge, where the chaotic facies is not related to the accretion of ophiolites or to the collisional processes but is the result of mud diapirs.
